passage:
Dear Lalremsiami,
Sorry for the late reply. Things here are the same. At home I am the sensible one. Papa says, “Seema will handle it,” about the water bill, my brother's lunch box and even Nani's medicine reminders. My brother Tinku broke the window again last week and everybody laughed, and Mummy said, “What to do, that is Tinku.” When I was late from tuition once, nobody laughed at all. I want to try out for the school choir, but Mummy said, “You don't like all that,” and I didn't argue. I love them. I am just tired of being sensible, and I wonder who I would be if I dropped the list for one day.
Seema

qa.q: What does Papa say Seema will handle?
qa.a: Papa says, “Seema will handle it,” about the water bill, the lunch box and Nani's medicine reminders.

qa.q: Why does Seema say, “I am just tired of being sensible”?
qa.a: Seema is worn out by the fixed role of the reliable one, which leaves no room to try things like the school choir, though Seema still says “I love them.”

qa.q: What could Seema do next about the choir?
qa.a: Seema could tell Mummy calmly that the choir matters, ask for one small chance to try, and perhaps ask Papa to share some of the chores.

qa.q: How might Tinku experience being the troublemaker?
qa.a: Tinku may feel labelled too, since everyone laughs it off, which could mean Tinku is not expected to be trusted with anything serious.

grounding: A teenager writes about being cast as the responsible one, which gives a place in the family and leaves little room for other sides.

passage: Okay, so, first question: who's the funny one? That's me, Naveen, the family joke. At dinner Dada says, “Naveen, say something silly,” and I do, because if I'm laughing, nobody's asking about my marks. My sister Ishita is the trusted one. If a vase breaks, they ask me first. Ishita never says anything. She just stares at her plate. Last week I got my best maths score, and Papa said, “Did you copy?” Everyone laughed, including me. I laughed loudest. The thing is, if I stop being funny, I don't know where I'd sit at that table.

qa.q: What did Papa ask when Naveen got the best maths score?
qa.a: Papa asked, “Did you copy?”

qa.q: Why does Naveen laugh loudest when the others laugh at the question?
qa.a: Naveen seems to use the joke role to cover hurt about not being trusted, and fears losing a place at the table if the joking stops.

qa.q: What could Naveen try at dinner to be seen as more than the funny one?
qa.a: Naveen could share something serious, like how the maths score was earned, or ask one family member to take it seriously.

qa.q: What might Ishita be thinking as she stares at her plate?
qa.a: Ishita may feel uncomfortable about the doubt aimed at Naveen and stuck in her own role, since she says nothing and looks down.

grounding: A teenager plays the family joker, which brings a place at the table and hides worry about being seen as the problem.

'Mohit, did you pay the electricity bill online?' Papa asked from the sofa.
'Done at lunch.'
'And the gas booking?'
'Tomorrow morning, first thing.'
Aadhya grinned. 'Our family manager. Tell Papa a joke, Mohit. Oh wait, you don't make jokes.'
Mausi laughed. 'Mohit is the serious one. Aadhya is our comedian.'
Mohit smiled back, but his jaw was tight. 'Actually, I signed up for the school drama club today.'
The room went quiet.
'Drama?' Papa said. 'With boards next year? Who will handle things here?'
'I can still do the bills.'
'Let Aadhya do the acting, beta. You're our steady one.'
Mohit looked down at his phone. 'Sure. Forget it.'
Later, Aadhya knocked on his door. 'I think you'd be good at it, you know.'

qa.q: What did Mohit sign up for at school?
qa.a: The school drama club.

qa.q: What does Mohit's tight jaw suggest while everyone laughs?
qa.a: He was uncomfortable and a bit hurt at being boxed in as 'the serious one', even while smiling along.

qa.q: What could Papa do differently when Mohit mentions the drama club?
qa.a: Ask what draws him to it and help him fit it around boards and chores, instead of reminding him of his 'steady' role.

qa.q: How does Aadhya seem to see Mohit's role by the end?
qa.a: She teased him with the family label at first, but later tells him he'd be good at acting, showing she sees more in him.

grounding: A teenager cast as the family's reliable one gains a secure place but is held back when he tries something new.

passage: Somewhere around Class 6, I became the family's 'problem'. If a glass broke at a function, my aunts looked at me before they looked at the floor. Last month at my cousin's wedding, the sound system cut out and an uncle shouted, 'Arohi, what did you touch?' I hadn't touched anything. But I rolled my eyes and said, 'Obviously me,' and everyone laughed, and it felt easier than arguing. The strange part is that at my friend Dilnaz's house, her parents call me 'the helpful one', because I always clear the table there. I like that version of me more. At home, though, it's like there's only one chair left for me, and it's the one near the door.

qa.q: What did the uncle shout when the sound system cut out?
qa.a: 'Arohi, what did you touch?'

qa.q: Why did Arohi say 'Obviously me' instead of arguing?
qa.a: Arohi felt resigned and tired of fighting the label, so joking along felt easier, even though Arohi hadn't touched anything.

qa.q: What could Arohi try to show the family a different side?
qa.a: Say calmly 'It wasn't me' next time, or talk to one trusted relative about wanting to be seen as helpful at home too.

qa.q: How do Dilnaz's parents see Arohi?
qa.a: They see Arohi as 'the helpful one', because Arohi always clears the table at their house.

grounding: A teenager plays along with the family's 'problem' label, which gives a place in the family but limits who they can be there.

passage: Counsellor's note, Thursday. Arnab (Class 10) came in after his class teacher mentioned he jokes through every serious moment. Today he joked about his own low marks, then went quiet. He said at home he is 'the entertainer' and his elder brother Ujjwal is 'the topper'. When his parents argue, he does funny voices until everyone laughs. 'If I stop, who will?' he asked. I told him that making people laugh is a real gift, and that he is also allowed to be worried, or serious, or bad at something without covering it with a joke. With his permission, I called his mother this afternoon and asked for a family meeting next week, with Ujjwal there too. His mother sounded surprised. 'But he's always so happy,' she said.

qa.q: What does Arnab do when his parents argue?
qa.a: He does funny voices until everyone laughs.

qa.q: What might Arnab be worried about when he asks 'If I stop, who will?'
qa.a: He seems anxious that without his jokes the family tension would have no relief, and that his place depends on being the entertainer.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do next, and why does it help?
qa.a: The counsellor called Arnab's mother, with his permission, and set up a family meeting with Ujjwal present, so the family can see the role he has been carrying.

qa.q: How might Arnab's mother see him before the meeting?
qa.a: She sees him as 'always so happy', so she is surprised; the jokes have hidden his worry from her.

grounding: A counsellor's note on a teenager locked into the family's 'entertainer' role, which gives him a place but hides his worries.

passage:
Saturday
Eshaan broke Papa's scooter mirror today, reversing into the gate. Big drama. Mummy shouted, Papa sighed, and then everyone turned to me like always: "Chaitanya, take it to the mechanic. You're the sensible one." So I did. I'm always the one who fills forms, remembers Dadi's appointments, calms everyone down. It's nice being the one they trust. Honestly, I like it.
But at the mechanic's I saw a poster for school drama auditions and thought, I'd love to try. Then: what would they say? "Chaitanya, acting? You?" Eshaan is the dramatic one. I'm the responsible one. There isn't room for two.
Tonight Eshaan came to my room and said sorry for making me run around. Then: "You'd be a good actor, you know. You fake being calm all the time."
I laughed. Then I took the audition form out of my bag again.

qa.q: What did Eshaan break?
qa.a: Papa's scooter mirror.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya feel about being "the sensible one"?
qa.a: Chaitanya feels proud and trusted, but also boxed in, longing to try acting and worried the family has no room for it.

qa.q: What small step could Chaitanya take outside the role?
qa.a: Go to the drama audition and tell the family plainly, while still being reliable in the ways Chaitanya chooses.

qa.q: How does Eshaan seem to see Chaitanya's role?
qa.a: Eshaan sees past it, noticing the calm is partly an act, and encourages Chaitanya to try something new.

grounding: Shows a teenager living out the family role of the reliable one, which gives a secure place but limits who they feel allowed to become.
